composing_text: 129th Infantry Brigade; 130th Infantry Brigade; 214th Infantry Brigade
notes: Landed about 24 June (Wikipedia list shows Juno); concentrated for Epsom.

current_activity: relieving Scottish infantry at Cheux; repulsing Panther attack
notes: Relieved Scottish infantry around Cheux and Sainte-Manvieu 27 June; a battalion position was counter-attacked by six 2nd Panzer Division Panthers at 09:30, attacks halted; reinforced 28 June by 32nd (Guards) Infantry Brigade; a brigade reinforced the Odon bridgehead 29 June.

current_activity: Jupiter: the reinforced division attacks Eterville, Maltot and Hill 112 at 05:00; on the slopes of the hill by 08:00
notes: Event date: 10 July 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, pp. 316, 317). Event definition: The 43rd Division, reinforced by the 4th Armoured, 31st Tank and 46th (Highland) Infantry Brigades, opens the attack to expand the Odon bridgehead at 05:00 on 10 July; its leading troops reach Eterville and are well up on the slopes of Hill 112 by 08:00 and the advance on Maltot follows (pp. 316-317). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, pp. 316-317: "The troops to be employed were the 43rd Division reinforced by the 4th Armoured, 31st Tank and 46th (Highland) Infantry Brigades"; "The attack was to open at 5 a.m. on the"; "leading troops of the 43rd Division reached Eterville and were well up on the slopes of Hill 112 by eight o". Location: Hill 112, Calvados (existing place PL0173) with a precision of 5 km. Location support: Ellis names Hill 112, Eterville and Maltot as the objectives and the slopes of Hill 112 as reached (pp. 316-317). Context: Ellis does not name the corps on these pages; the corps is the standing relation of the division in the dataset (VIII Corps, CR0074), which the Wikipedia infobox of Jupiter (R597) also gives.

current_activity: Bluecoat: develops a 'right hook' against Cahagnes at first light and takes the village in the afternoon
notes: Event date: 31 July 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 392). Event definition: By first light on 31 July troops of the division, developing a 'right hook' against Cahagnes, are within striking distance when a sharp German counter-attack is driven off; Cahagnes is taken during the afternoon and late that night St. Pierre-du-Fresne is entered (p. 392); on 1 August the division continues to Point 361 (p. 392). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 392: "by first light on the morning of the 31st troops of its 43rd Division, developing a"; "Cahagnes was taken during the afternoon". Location: Cahagnes, Calvados (existing place PL0062) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Ellis names Cahagnes as taken during the afternoon (p. 392).

current_activity: Mont Pincon: attacks the west face at 14:30; tanks on the top by eight o'clock; garrison eliminated by morning
notes: Event date: 6 August 1944, 14:30 (Ellis, vol. I, pp. 409, 410). Event definition: After securing Ondefontaine on 5 August the division attacks the west face of Mont Pincon at 14:30 on 6 August with the 129th Brigade, the 130th Brigade assaulting the north face from Ondefontaine; seven tanks climb to the top and the rest of the squadron joins them by eight o'clock, two infantry battalions of the 129th Brigade reach the hill in the fog, and the garrison is eliminated when the fog clears in the early morning of 7 August (pp. 409-410). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 409: "The attack began at half past two on the 6th"; p. 410: "When the fog cleared in the early morning the garrison was elimin- ated and two hundred prisoners were taken". Location: Mont Pincon, Calvados (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Ellis names Mont Pincon (Point 361 and the hill) as the objective and the place taken (pp. 409-410).

current_activity: Crosses the Seine at Vernon in stormboats; seven of the first eight boats are lost
notes: Event date: 25 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 466). Event definition: Fifteen minutes after the corps guns open fire across the Seine from Vernon on 25 August, the first troops of the division cross in stormboats; seven of the eight boats are lost to fire from the far bank, but a battalion and a half cross during the night and fight off a number of attacks (p. 466). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 466: "the first British troops began to cross the river in stormboats"; "In spite of these mishaps a battalion and a half crossed during the night". Location: Vernon, Eure (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Ellis names Vernon as the crossing place and the 43rd Division as the unit (p. 466).

current_activity: Clipper: attacks on the left of the US 84th Division at Geilenkirchen; Geilenkirchen falls the next day
notes: Event date: 18 November 1944 (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 161, 162). Event definition: On 18 November, after the United States 84th Division has attacked on the right and passed the Siegfried Line pill-boxes by midday, the 43rd Division attacks on its left in the XXX Corps attack astride the Wurm river; many tanks, carriers and other vehicles bog down off the roads; Geilenkirchen is captured the next day after a stiff fight (the page does not say which unit took it), and two days later a battalion of the 10th SS Panzer Division attacks the 43rd Division in a hard fight (pp. 161-162). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, pp. 161-162: "the British 43rd Division then attacked on its left"; "Next day Geilenkirchen was captured after a stiff fight"; "Two days later a battalion of the roth SS Panzer Division attacked the 43rd Division and a hard fight ensued". Location: Geilenkirchen, North Rhine-Westphalia (existing place PL0558) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the town of Geilenkirchen; the division fought on the left (north) of the American division and its headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names the attack on Geilenkirchen and the Wurm villages and puts the division on the left of the American division (p. 161). Context: Flagged addition: a 1944 row added in British Batch 2 only so that the existing OP-CLIPPER has a second British claim; Ellis does not name the operation.

current_activity: Blackcock: comes into action on the 52nd Division right; drives up to the Wurm and meets the US XIII Corps
notes: Event date: 24 January 1945 (the page gives no day for the advance: the sentence is in the account of the 24th) (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 245, 246, 247, 248). Event definition: In Operation Blackcock the division comes into action on the right of the 52nd Division while the latter forces the second German defence line on a front of about two miles (about 21 January); in the mopping-up of the 24th, on the opposite flank from the 7th Armoured Division, it drives up to the Wurm, making contact with troops of the United States XIII Corps, who have begun to move forward along the right bank of the river (pp. 245-246). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 245: "supplemented by the advance of the 43rd Division which had just come into action on its right"; pp. 246-248: "On the opposite flank the 43rd Division drove up to the Wurm, making contact with troops of the United States XIII Corps who had begun to move forward along the right bank of the river". Location: Geilenkirchen, North Rhine-Westphalia (existing place PL0558), at the southern end of the corps front on the Wurm with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is Geilenkirchen, just south of the stretch of the Wurm the division reached; the page names no village; the division headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis puts the Wurm at the right (southern) end of the XII Corps front, just north of Geilenkirchen (p. 242), and the division on that flank (p. 246).

current_activity: Veritable: passes through for Goch, Udem and Weeze; the 129th Brigade is in Cleve at first light and pinned down all day
notes: Event date: the evening of 9 February to 10 February 1945 (Ellis, vol. II, p. 262). Event definition: Having heard that the Materborn feature has been seized, General Horrocks orders the 43rd Division, with the 8th Armoured Brigade under command, to start from Nijmegen at 19:00 on 9 February and pass through the 15th Division for Goch, Udem and Weeze; the 129th Brigade leads along the road through Kranenburg to Nutterden, taking three hours for the ten miles, and the leading battalion reaches Cleve shortly after first light on the 10th; the whole brigade is involved in bitter fighting all day and is pinned down among the ruins of Cleve, and the 214th Brigade is stopped for several hours in Nutterden in a jam (pp. 262-263). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 262: "General Horrocks had ordered the 43rd Division to start from Nijmegen at 7 p.m. and to pass through the 15th for Goch, Udem and Weeze"; "the leading battalion reached Cleve shortly after first light"; "the brigade group was pinned down among the ruins of Cleve". Location: Cleve, North Rhine-Westphalia (existing place PL0578) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the town centre of Cleve, where the leading brigade was pinned down; the division headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names Cleve as the town the leading brigade reached and fought in (p. 262).

current_activity: Veritable: night attack breaks through the 15th Panzer Grenadier Division, takes the escarpment north-east of Goch
notes: Event date: 17 February 1945 (a night attack) (Ellis, vol. II, p. 267). Event definition: After the 15th Division has taken Cleve the 43rd Division, avoiding the Cleve Forest and skirting Pfalzdorf, which is about to fall to the 53rd, heads for the escarpment north-east of Goch; in heavy fighting by each of its brigades in turn it breaks through the 15th Panzer Grenadier Division and in a vigorous night attack covers four or five miles to secure the escarpment on 17 February and cut the Goch-Calcar road, which General Horrocks afterwards describes as the turning point in the battle; after dark the divisional engineers open seven crossings over the outer anti-tank ditch at the foot of the escarpment (p. 267). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 267: "the 43rd Division headed for the escarpment north-east of Goch"; "to secure the escarpment on the 17th and also to cut the Goch". Location: Goch, North Rhine-Westphalia (new place), the town the escarpment overlooks with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the town of Goch; the escarpment lies about a mile or so to the north-east and the division headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names the escarpment as about a mile from Goch on the north, overlooking the town (p. 267).

current_activity: Blockbuster: takes over the ground on the Canadian left, secures Calcar and moves on towards Marienbaum
notes: Event date: 3 March 1945 (Ellis, vol. II, p. 274). Event definition: As the 2nd Canadian Division and the 4th Armoured Division fight to open the Hochwald gap (by the night of 3 March), the 43rd Division takes over the ground gained on the Canadians' left and secures Calcar; while the division moves on towards Marienbaum, its reconnaissance regiment and sappers, working mostly by night, mop up enemy detachments between the Calcar-Xanten road and the Rhine (p. 274). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 274: "the 43rd Division took over the ground gained by the Canadians' left, and secured Calcar"; "While the division moved on towards Marienbaun". Location: Calcar, North Rhine-Westphalia (existing place PL0705) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the town of Calcar; the division headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names Calcar as the town secured (p. 274).

current_activity: Plunder: comes into action on the night of 26 March and captures Megchelen (Ellis: Mechelen) early on the 28th
notes: Event date: 28 March 1945, early (Ellis, vol. II, p. 293). Event definition: On the night of 26-27 March the division comes into action in the XXX Corps bridgehead at Rees and goes on to capture Mechelen early on 28 March, by which time most of the 3rd Canadian Division is across the Rhine and advancing west to take Emmerich and the 51st Division has secured Isselburg (Ellis, vol. II, p. 293); the village named Mechelen is the Dutch village of Megchelen, just over the Dutch frontier, which a local-history foundation records as entered by part of the Wessex Division on the morning of 28 March, after it had fought its way through Millingen on 26-27 March (Opdat Wij Niet Vergeten). Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and a Dutch local-history foundation, Opdat Wij Niet Vergeten). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, pp. 293-295: "That night the 43rd Division came into action and went on to capture Mechelen early on the 28th"; "the 51st Division had secured Isselburg"; Opdat Wij Niet Vergeten, "Megchelen bevrijd": "In de ochtend van 28 maart glipt een deel van de Wessex Divisie langs de Duitse flank en dringt, vlak over de Nederlandse grens, Megchelen binnen"; "Megchelen in de Tweede Wereldoorlog": "Op de ochtend van 28 maart 1945 bereikten Britse troepen Megchelen". Location: Megchelen, Gelderland (new place), the village just over the Dutch frontier with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the village of Megchelen; the division headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names Mechelen between the Rhine bridgehead at Rees, Isselburg and Emmerich (p. 293); the local-history pages place the 43rd Division in Megchelen on the morning of 28 March. Commander: Maj.-Gen. G. I. Thomas, commanding the 43rd (Wessex) Division (Ellis, vol. II, p. 375). Context: Review (British Batch 2 follow-up, 28 October 2026; the place name is an identification): Ellis spells the village Mechelen, which is the Dutch Megchelen; Ellis names it once, on p. 293. The context (the 43rd Division advancing from Rees through Millingen towards Isselburg, Emmerich on the left) and the local-history pages that give Megchelen on 28 March place it at Megchelen. No other place of that name lies on the road from the Rhine bridgehead at Rees to Isselburg and Emmerich. The row is kept at 0.7 because the day and the unit are in Ellis and the village is confirmed by the second source.

current_activity: Bremen: liquidates the hard core of opposition round the garrison headquarters in the night; the commander is captured
notes: Event date: the night of 26 April 1945 (Ellis, vol. II, p. 316). Event definition: After the city has been assaulted on 25 April, German resistance is thoroughly shaken and only round the garrison headquarters is a hard core of opposition met; the 43rd Division liquidates this during the night of 26 April; the garrison commander and the commander of the city's defence are captured and the city is clear of the enemy by the 27th (p. 316). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 316: "only round the garrison headquarters was a hard core of opposition met; this was liquidated by the 43rd Division during the night of the 26th"; "The garrison commander and the com- mander of the city's defence were captured and the city was clear of the enemy by the 27th". Location: Bremen (existing place PL0625) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the city of Bremen; the garrison headquarters is not located on the page and the division headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names Bremen and its garrison headquarters (p. 316).
